name: WALK THIS WAIOLI BURGER (comes with Wasabi Aioli)

recipe.history:
Wasabi — Wasabia japonica — is one of the most difficult and expensive crops in the world to cultivate, requiring cold, fast-moving mountain stream water, high humidity, and years of patient growing before the rhizome reaches harvestable size. Native to Japan, it has been used in Japanese cuisine for over a thousand years, appearing in historical records as both a condiment and a medicinal herb believed to neutralize the bacteria present in raw fish. True wasabi, freshly grated on a sharkskin grater called an oroshigane, is a fleeting experience — its pungent, sinus-clearing heat is entirely different from the burn of chili peppers, coming from volatile isothiocyanate compounds that dissipate within fifteen minutes of grating. The wasabi served in most Western sushi restaurants is actually a blend of horseradish, mustard, and green food coloring, a substitute born of the fact that fresh Wasabia japonica is extraordinarily scarce and expensive outside Japan. Real or approximated, wasabi carries the weight of Japanese culinary philosophy — restraint, precision, and the idea that a condiment should elevate, not overwhelm.

Aioli — the great emulsified garlic sauce of the western Mediterranean — met wasabi in the fusion kitchens of 1990s California and the result was an instant classic of cross-cultural condiment invention. French and Provençal aioli, built on garlic, olive oil, and egg yolk, had already been absorbed into the American culinary vocabulary by way of the California cuisine movement championed by Alice Waters and her contemporaries. When Japanese ingredients began flooding restaurant pantries during the sushi boom of the 1980s and 1990s, creative chefs started spiking their aioli with wasabi paste, creating a condiment with the richness of mayonnaise, the gentle garlic depth of traditional aioli, and a sinus-lifting heat that made it unlike anything in the European tradition. On a burger, wasabi aioli punches through the fat of the beef and the richness of the cheese, providing brightness and heat without acidity, a kind of condiment clarity that elevates the whole assembly.

The first time I made wasabi aioli was an accident. I was trying to clear my refrigerator before a long weekend and I had a tube of wasabi paste, a bowl of leftover aioli from a dinner party, and a desperate need to make something interesting out of a plain patty. I stirred a generous squeeze of wasabi into the aioli, tasted it off my finger, and stood very still for a moment while the heat moved through my sinuses and the rich garlic creaminess settled behind it. I remember thinking: this is exactly what a burger needs when everything else about it is correct but it needs one more thing. I spread it on both buns, built the burger, and took a bite that I still think about years later. That clean, sharp heat cutting through the beef fat is one of those flavor combinations that feels obvious only after you've experienced it.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — that internal temperature window of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — is the act of treating beef with the same respect that a Japanese chef treats a piece of sashimi-grade fish. You are working with an exceptional ingredient and your job is to apply just enough heat to transform it while preserving everything that makes it worth eating. The wasabi in this aioli demands that standard. A dry, overcooked patty cannot hold its own against a condiment this vibrant — the wasabi would simply taste harsh against gray, squeezed-out meat. At medium rare, the beef's fat and juices are fully present, the interior is pink and warm, and the wasabi aioli finds a partner worthy of its intensity. Medium rare is not a preference; it is the only temperature at which this particular burger makes complete sense.
ingredients: 1 egg + 1 tbsp water for egg wash
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend), freshly ground
2 to 3 tsp wasabi paste (adjust to heat preference)
1 small cucumber, thinly sliced into rounds
pinch of sugar and salt for cabbage slaw
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add egg and softened butter. Mix briefly. Add bread flour and salt. Knead with dough hook on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
4. Divide into 4 portions (~150g each), shape into tight rounds, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle with black sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a rack.

6. Make the wasabi aioli: Roast garlic cloves in a dry pan over low heat until soft and fragrant, about 8 minutes. Peel and mash to a paste. Whisk together egg yolks, Dijon mustard, lemon juice, and rice wine vinegar in a bowl. While whisking constantly, add neutral oil in a very slow, thin stream until fully emulsified into a thick mayonnaise. Whisk in garlic paste, wasabi paste, and soy sauce. Taste and adjust wasabi and salt. Refrigerate until needed.
7. Make the slaw: Toss shredded napa cabbage with sesame oil, rice wine vinegar, sugar, and a pinch of salt. Let sit 10 minutes to soften slightly.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (170g each). Form into 3/4-inch thick patties with a center dimple. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.
9. Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil.
10. Place patties in the pan. Cook 2 minutes undisturbed. Flip once. Top each patty with a slice of pepper jack cheese immediately.
11. Cook 1.5 to 2 minutes more, tenting with foil, until an instant-read thermometer reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
12. Toast the buns: Butter cut sides and toast face-down in a skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1 minute.
13. Assemble: Spread wasabi aioli generously on both cut faces of each bun.
14. Pile the sesame-vinegar slaw on the bottom bun. Add cucumber rounds and radish slices.
15. Place the medium-rare pepper jack patty on top. Scatter sliced scallions over the patty.
16. Spread an extra small dollop of wasabi aioli on the underside of the top bun. Cap and serve immediately.
